questions.q: If $f(x+y)=f(x) \cdot f(y), f(3)=3, f^{\prime}(0)=11$, then $f^{\prime}(3)$ is equal to
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& f^{\prime}(3)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(3+h)-f(3)}{h} \\
& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(3) f(h)-f(3)}{h} \quad[\because f(x+y)=f(x) f(y)]
\end{aligned}$
Now, $f(x+0)=f(x) \cdot f(0)\Rightarrow f(x)[f(0)-1]=0$
Either f(x)=0 or $f(0)=1\begin{aligned}
\therefore f^{\prime}(3) & =f(3) \lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h} \\
& =f(3) f^{\prime}(0)=f(3) \cdot 11 \\
& =3 \times 11=33
\end{aligned}$

Now, $\log _\theta\{$(x+1)(x+2)\}$ is defined, if

Clearly, $x=-$\frac{5}{3}  does not satisfy this condition. But all other values of $x satisfy the above conditions. Hence, the number of solutions lying in the domain of definition of the given function is 3.

questions.solution:

questions.q: Let $f(x y)=f(x) \cdot f(y)$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$. If $f^{\prime}(1)=2$ and $f(4)=4$, then $f^{\prime}(4)$ equal to
questions.solution:
We have $f(x y)=f(x) f(y)$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.
Putting $x=y=1$, we get
$f(1)=f(1) f(1)\Rightarrow f(1)[1-f(1)]=0\Rightarrow \quad f(1)=1 \quad[\because f(1) \neq 0] \quad \ldots(i)$
Now, $f^{\prime}(1)=2\Rightarrow \quad \lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}=2\Rightarrow \quad f(1) \lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(h)-1}{h}=2\Rightarrow \quad \lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(1) f(h)-f(1)}{h}=2 \quad[$ using $f(1)=1]$...(ii)
$\Rightarrow \quad \lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(h)-1}{h}=2$
Now $f^{\prime}(4)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(4+h)-f(4)}{h}=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(4) \cdot f(h)-f(4)}{h}=\left\{\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(h)-1}{h}\right\} \cdot f(4)=2 f(4) \quad\{ from $(i)\}=2 \times 4=8

questions.solution:
Total number of mappings from a set $A$ having elements into itself is $n^n$.
And the total number of one to one mapping is $n!\therefore$ Required probability $=\frac{n!}{n^n}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The function $f(x)=\max \{(1-x),(1+x), 2\}$, $x \in(-\infty, \infty)$ is equivalent to
questions.solution:
Given that,
$f(x)=\max \{(1-x), 2,(1+x)\}$
For $x \leq-1$, we find that $1-x \geq 2$ and $1-x \geq 1+x\therefore \max \{(1-x), 2,(1+x)\}=1-x$
For $-1 < x < 1$, we find that
$0 < 1-x < 2$ and $0 < 1+x < 2\therefore \max \{(1-x), 2,(1+x)\}=2$
For $x \geq 1$, we find that
$1+x \geq 2,1+x>1-x\therefore \max \{(1-x), 2,(1+x)\}=1+x$
Hence, $f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{cc}1-x, & x \leq-1 \\ 2, & -1 < x < 1 \\ 1+x, & x \geq 1\end{array}\right.$
